parts.stem: How is the strange sound described?
options: like the sound of the wind
like the sound of cane-cards on the buffalo blanket
like the sound of pine trees
like the sound of Mitsina grumbling
parts.hint: Find the sentence that says what the warrior heard from outside Mitsina’s house.

steps.explain: Check the other options.

B — the cane-cards on the blanket make the sound, but the passage does not say the sound is LIKE that.

D — nothing says Mitsina grumbles.

questions.stem:
Read this short passage.

When people took over the territory of the fairy penguins, it could have meant their extinction.

Source: Edel Wignell, The Portland Fairy Penguins, Sydney, Harcourt Brace Jovanovich, 1990

Which word best gives the meaning of TERRITORY?
questions.hint: Think about what the penguins lose if people take over their territory. Where do the penguins live and find their food?

steps.explain: Read the sentence with the word in it.
steps.work: “When people took over the territory of the fairy penguins, it could have meant their extinction.”

steps.explain: Think about what the penguins need.
steps.work: Penguins need a place where they live, find food and raise their young. If people take it over, the penguins could die out.

steps.explain: Check each option.
steps.work:
acres — a measure of land size.

fields — land used for crops or animals, not for wild penguins.

nests — only the small places where eggs are laid, which is too small.

habitat — the natural home area of an animal. ✓

steps.explain: Territory and habitat both mean the area an animal lives in.
steps.work: The answer is C.

keyPoints.note: Territory is the area an animal lives in. Look for the word that means the same.

questions.stem: AEROPLANE is to FLIGHT PATH as MOTOR VEHICLE is to ?
questions.hint: A flight path is the way an aeroplane travels from one place to another. What do we call the way a car travels from one place to another?

steps.explain: Find the link in the first pair.
steps.work: An AEROPLANE follows a FLIGHT PATH: the line it travels along from where it starts to where it lands. (vehicle → the path it follows)

steps.explain: Use the same link for MOTOR VEHICLE. What path does a car follow from start to finish?
steps.work: A car follows a ROUTE: the way a driver chooses to get from one place to another.

steps.explain: Check the other options.
steps.work:
A highway and a road are the physical things a car drives on. A flight path is not a physical thing in the sky, it is the chosen way to travel, just like a route.

A map only shows places, it is not a path a car follows.

steps.explain: AEROPLANE : FLIGHT PATH matches MOTOR VEHICLE : ROUTE.
steps.work: The answer is B.

keyPoints.note: A flight path is a way of travelling, not a thing on the ground. Find the matching word for a car.

questions.stem: When they are rearranged these letters will make a word that means FABLES. Which letters will make this word?
questions.hint: Think of another word for “fables”: old stories about gods and heroes. Then check whether its letters can be found in an option.

steps.work: Fables are old stories. A word with a similar meaning is MYTHS (old stories about gods and heroes).

steps.explain: Check that MYTHS can be made from the letters of one option.

MYTHS = M, Y, T, H, S

THYMS = T, H, Y, M, S — the same five letters!

questions.stem:
Questions 5 to 9 refer to the following passage.

THE PARABLE OF THE TEN GIRLS

Once there were ten girls who took their oil lamps and went out to meet the bridegroom. Five of them were foolish, and the other five were wise. The foolish ones took their lamps but did not take any extra oil with them, while the wise ones took containers full of oil for their lamps. The bridegroom was late in coming, so the girls began to nod and fall asleep.

It was already midnight when the cry rang out, ‘Here is the bridegroom! Come and meet him!’ The ten girls woke up and trimmed their lamps. Then the foolish ones said to the wise ones, ‘Let us have some of your oil, because our lamps are going out.’ ‘No indeed,’ the wise ones answered, ‘there is not enough for you and for us. Go to the shop and buy some for yourselves.’ So the foolish girls went off to buy some oil; and while they were gone, the bridegroom arrived. The five girls who were ready went in with him to the wedding feast, and the door was closed.

Later the other girls arrived. ‘Sir, sir! Let us in!’ they cried out. ‘Certainly not! I don’t know you,’ the bridegroom answered.

Source: Matthew, Chapter 25, verses 1–12, Today’s English Version, New York, American Bible Society, 1976

parts.stem: Why is this called a parable?
options: it is a story that uses an example to teach a lesson
it is a story from ancient life and times
it is a religious story and fable
it is a true story that teaches a lesson
parts.hint: A parable is a special kind of story. Look at how this story uses ten girls and their lamps to make a point.

steps.explain: Look at what happens in the story.
steps.work: Five girls are foolish and do not bring extra oil. Five girls are wise and do bring it. Only the wise girls are let in.

steps.explain: Ask what the story is really teaching.
steps.work: It is not really about lamps and oil. It uses the girls as an EXAMPLE to teach a lesson: be ready and prepared.

steps.explain: Check the other options.
steps.work:
B — many old stories come from ancient times, but that does not make them parables.

C — it is religious, but “fable” is a story with talking animals.

D — a parable is not a true event, it is a made-up story.

steps.explain: A parable is a story that uses an example to teach a lesson.
steps.work: The answer is A.

keyPoints.text: Why is this called a parable
keyPoints.note: A parable uses a simple made-up story as an example to teach a lesson.

parts.stem: How do we know that this parable is not from modern times?
options: the girls had to wait for the arrival of the bridegroom
the oil was carried around in containers
the parable was used only in ancient times
parts.hint: Look for something in the story that people do not use any more today.

steps.explain: Read the story for things that belong to the past.
steps.work:
“Once there were ten girls who took their oil lamps…”

Today we use electric lights and torches. Oil lamps point to old times.

steps.explain: Check the other options.
steps.work:
A — people wait for others today too.

C — we still carry oil and liquids in containers today.

D — this is not something the story tells us, and parables are still told today.

steps.explain: The oil lamps show that the story is from the past.
steps.work: The answer is B.

keyPoints.note: Find something in the story that people no longer use today.

parts.stem: What does the parable say about the bridegroom?
options: he claimed that he did not know the foolish girls
he expected to be met by the ten girls
parts.hint: Find the bridegroom’s own words at the end of the parable.

steps.explain: Find what the bridegroom says.
steps.work:
“‘Certainly not! I don’t know you,’ the bridegroom answered.”

He says this to the foolish girls who arrive late.

steps.explain: Check the other options.
steps.work:
A — the story does not talk about respect.

B — the bridegroom was late, not early (“The bridegroom was late in coming”).

D — he was expected by the ten girls, but the parable does not say what he expected.

steps.explain: The bridegroom said that he did not know the foolish girls.
steps.work: The answer is C.

parts.stem: What does the parable say about the wise girls?
options: they expected the bridegroom to be late
they were just thinking of themselves
they were able to get their lamps going in time
they were allowed into the wedding feast
parts.hint: Find what happens to the five wise girls when the bridegroom arrives.

steps.explain: Find the sentence about the wise girls going in.
steps.work:
“The five girls who were ready went in with him to the wedding feast, and the door was closed.”

The five who were ready are the wise girls.

steps.explain: Check the other options.
steps.work:
A — the story says they brought extra oil, but it does not say why.

B — the story does not say they were selfish, only that there was not enough oil to share.

C — the story does not say they got their lamps going; it says they “trimmed their lamps”.

steps.explain: The wise girls were allowed into the wedding feast.
steps.work: The answer is D.

parts.stem: What do you think is the main point of this parable?
options: this is a story about the problems of not being punctual
this is a story that shows being ready for everything is rewarded
this is a story about being prepared
this is a story about five wise and five foolish girls
parts.hint: The main point is the lesson of the story. Which option says that being ready is rewarded, including what happened to the ones who were ready and the ones who were not?

steps.explain: Think about what happened to each group.
steps.work: The wise girls were prepared (they had extra oil) and were let in. The foolish girls were not prepared and were shut out.

steps.explain: The lesson must say what is rewarded, not only what the story is about.
steps.work:
A — it is about the bridegroom being late, not about being punctual.

C — “being prepared” is true, but it does not say what the story shows about being prepared.

D — this only says who is in the story.

B — being ready for everything is rewarded. ✓

steps.explain: The answer is B.

keyPoints.note: The main point is the lesson the story teaches, not just what happens in it.

questions.stem:
Questions 20 to 24 refer to the following passage.

THE STORY OF ARTHUR STACE

Eternity

A short, grey-haired and lightly built man, who looked quite frail, would often be seen in the early mornings around Wynyard Station. They say that he was always dressed the same, with a grey felt hat, tie and double-breasted navy blue suit.

He began early, usually before dawn, and he wandered through many of the inner Sydney suburbs. As he walked every so often he would stop, pull out a chalk, bend down and write on the footpath in large, neat running-writing — ETERNITY. He would walk a further hundred metres then write it again, ETERNITY, nothing else, only one word. For 37 years he chalked this one-word message to the whole of Sydney and he wrote it more than half a million times.

For many years the writer of these ‘Eternity’ signs was anonymous. It mystified Sydney. He did not like publicity and the mystery of the unknown writer of ETERNITY only became clear in 1956. One day Rev. Lisle Thompson, who knew Stace as a church cleaner, saw him take out his chalk and write the well-known ‘Eternity’ sign on the footpath. He did it without realising that he had been spotted. Arthur Stace died of a stroke in a nursing home on July 30, 1967. He was 83.

Sources: Reverend Lisle M. Thompson, The Crooked Made Straight, St Barnabas web site; transcript of a book by Keith Dunstan, Ratbags

parts.stem: What is the main idea of the article?
options: how the writer of ‘Eternity’ was discovered
the lifetime work of a man
some publicity for the writer of ‘Eternity’
parts.hint: The main idea covers the whole article. The article is about a man and what he did for most of his life.

steps.explain: Say what each paragraph is about.
steps.work:
Paragraph 1: what Arthur Stace looked like.

Paragraph 2: what he did every morning — wrote ETERNITY on the footpaths for 37 years.

Paragraph 3: the mystery of who the writer was, and how he was found.

steps.explain: Find the idea that covers all three paragraphs.
steps.work: The article tells the story of a man and the one-word message he chalked for 37 years — his lifetime work.

steps.explain: Check the other options.
steps.work:
A — only paragraph 3 is about being discovered.

C — religion is only mentioned briefly.

D — Stace did not like publicity.

steps.explain: The answer is B.

keyPoints.note: The main idea must cover the whole article, not just one paragraph.

meta.source: Excel Practice Opportunity Class Tests · Year 4

parts.stem: What can we judge about the man who wrote ‘Eternity’?
options: he was a minister of religion
parts.hint: Judge him from what the article says he did and did not like. Did he want to be famous?

steps.explain: Find the clues about how he behaved.
steps.work: “He did not like publicity…” and “…without realising that he had been spotted.” He wrote for 37 years without asking for any credit.

steps.explain: What kind of person does not want credit for work he does?
steps.work: A humble person — someone who is not boastful and does not need to be praised.

steps.explain: Check the other options.
steps.work:
B — nothing says he was poor.

C — he was unknown for many years, but this is a fact, not a judgement about him as a person.

D — he was a church cleaner, not a minister.

steps.explain: The answer is A.

keyPoints.note: To judge means to work out what kind of person he was from clues in the article.

parts.stem: Why did Arthur Stace write ‘Eternity’ on the footpaths of Sydney?

he wanted to keep active and do something worthwhile
he wanted to send a message to the people of Sydney
he wanted to do more than just be a church cleaner
parts.hint: Find the sentence that says what the word ETERNITY was meant to be.

steps.explain: Find the sentence about the message.
steps.work: “For 37 years he chalked this one-word message to the whole of Sydney…”

steps.explain: So what was he doing when he wrote the word?
steps.work: He was sending a message to the people of Sydney.

steps.explain: Check the other options.
steps.work: A, B and D are guesses about why he did it. The article only states that it was a message to the whole of Sydney.

steps.explain: The answer is C.

keyPoints.note: The reason is stated in the article. Find the word “message”.

parts.stem: Where was Stace often seen?

steps.explain: Check the other options.
steps.work:
B and D — he wandered through many of the inner Sydney suburbs, but he was not “often” seen at one place there.

C — this is what he did, not where he was.

steps.explain: The answer is A.

parts.stem: Which word gives the best meaning of ETERNITY?
parts.hint: Eternity means time that never ends. Which word means “lasting for ever”?

steps.explain: Say what ETERNITY means.
steps.work: Eternity is time without end — it goes on for ever.

steps.explain: Check each option.
steps.work:
unchanging — stays the same, but could still end.

constant — continues without stopping, but not necessarily for ever.

permanent — lasts a very long time, but is still not “for ever”.

everlasting — lasting for ever. ✓

steps.explain: The answer is D.

questions.stem:
This is a chart which shows the top ten selling cars last year. They are listed in alphabetical order.

| Car | Sold |
|---|---|
| Camry | 42 031 |
| Commodore | 107 514 |
| Corolla | 25 079 |
| Excel | 44 016 |
| Falcon | 79 615 |
| Festiva | 20 170 |
| Lancer | 17 161 |
| Magna | 35 644 |
| Pulsar | 19 835 |
| Starlet | 16 283 |

Source: VFACTS

Which was the fifth highest selling car in Australia?
questions.hint: The cars are in ABC order, not number order. Put the sales numbers in order from the biggest to the smallest, then count along to the fifth one.

steps.explain: Read the question carefully: the fifth HIGHEST, so we must rank the cars from the biggest number to the smallest.
steps.work: The table is in alphabetical order, so the 5th row (Falcon) is not the 5th highest.

steps.explain: Find the largest numbers first. Only one number has six digits, then compare the five-digit numbers.

questions.stem:
Which number comes next in the series?

2  3  5  8  13  21  ?
questions.hint: Work out how much is added each time: 1, 2, 3, 5, … Do these gaps look like the numbers in the series itself?

steps.explain: Find the gap between each pair of neighbouring numbers.
steps.work: \(2\rightarrow3\) is \(+1\), \(3\rightarrow5\) is \(+2\), \(5\rightarrow8\) is \(+3\), \(8\rightarrow13\) is \(+5\), \(13\rightarrow21\) is \(+8\).

questions.stem: It cost \(\$44\) for one adult and one child to visit an amusement park and \(\$58\) for one adult and two children. How much is the cost for one adult to visit the amusement park?
questions.hint: Compare the two prices. What is different about the two groups of people, and how much more does the second group cost?

steps.explain: Write the two facts so they can be compared. Both groups have one adult; the second group has one more child.
steps.work:
1 adult + 1 child \(=\$44\)

1 adult + 2 children \(=\$58\)

questions.stem: You have 71 square tiles for an area. Make these into the largest possible square area using as many of the tiles as you can. How many tiles would you have left over?
questions.hint: A square area uses a square number of tiles: 1, 4, 9, 16, … Find the biggest square number that is not more than 71.

steps.explain: A square made of tiles has the same number of tiles along each side, so it uses a square number of tiles. List the square numbers near 71.
81 is more than 71, so 9 by 9 is too big. The largest square we can make is 8 tiles by 8 tiles.
steps.work: \(8\times8=64\) tiles

questions.stem: Sixty-four stamps cost \(\$28.80\). Which calculation do you use to work out the cost of one stamp?
questions.hint: To find the cost of ONE item when you know the total cost, share the total equally between all the items. Which operation shares equally?

steps.explain: Decide what we know and what we want to find.
steps.work:
Known: total cost \(=\$28.80\) for 64 stamps.

Wanted: the cost of 1 stamp.

steps.explain: Sharing a total equally between 64 stamps is division.
steps.work: cost of 1 stamp \(=\) total cost \(\div\) number of stamps \(=\$28.80\div64\)

steps.explain: Check the other options.
steps.work:
A: \(45\text{c}\times64\) already uses the price of one stamp (45c), which we are trying to find — it would give the total.

C: \(64\div\$28.80\) divides the number of stamps by money.

D: \(64\times\$28.80\) would be the cost of 64 stamps if each stamp cost \(\$28.80\).

steps.explain: Work it out to see why A shows up as an option.
steps.work: \(28.80\div64=0.45\), so one stamp costs \(45\text{c}\). The calculation to use is \(\$28.80\div64\), option B.

keyPoints.note: You want the price of ONE: divide the total cost by the number of items.

questions.stem: Each shelf can hold up to five packets. How many shelves will I need to store nineteen packets?
questions.hint: Share the packets out five at a time. How many full shelves can you make, and what happens to the packets that are left over?

steps.explain: Each shelf holds at most 5 packets, so divide the 19 packets into groups of 5.
steps.work:
\(19\div5=3\) remainder \(4\)

3 full shelves hold \(3\times5=15\) packets. 4 packets are left over.

steps.explain: The 4 left-over packets still have to be stored, so they need one more shelf.

questions.stem:
What is the largest number that you can make from these seven digits?

1  1  3  5  8  2  9
questions.hint: The biggest digit in the first place makes the biggest number. Compare the four options place by place, from the left.

steps.explain: All four options use the same seven digits. To find which is the largest, compare them from the left, one place at a time.
The first digit is 5 in every option, and the second is 1 in every option. Now look at the third digit.
steps.work:
A has 1, B has 9, C has 1, D has 9.

A and C are smaller, so they are out. B and D both have 9.

steps.explain: Compare B and D at the fourth digit.
steps.work:
B 5 1 9 1 8 3 2 → the fourth digit is 1

D 5 1 9 2 8 1 3 → the fourth digit is 2

2 is greater than 1, so D is larger than B.

steps.explain: The largest of the numbers on offer is 5 192 813.
steps.work:
Note: if you could use the digits in any order, the largest number would be 9 853 211. It is not one of the options, so choose the largest option on the list.

The answer is D.

keyPoints.note: Compare the numbers from the left: the first place where they differ decides which is bigger.

questions.stem: At an exhibition there were 432 men, 368 women and 59 children. Then 68 men, 32 women and 9 children left. How do we calculate how many remained?
questions.hint: People who left must be taken away, not added. Work out the total at the start, the total who left, and then subtract.

steps.explain: Find the total number of people at the start.
Find the total number who left.
The people who remained are the ones at the start take away the ones who left.
Check the options: the calculation must use subtraction between the two totals, and the result must be 750.
steps.work:
A gives \(850\) and C gives \(650\) — wrong results.

D adds the people who left, which is wrong.

B: \((432+368+59)-(68+32+9)=750\) ✓

steps.explain: The answer is B.

keyPoints.note: People who left are taken away from the number at the start.
Remained means how many are still there, so subtract.

questions.stem:
Look at this clock. It is afternoon.

How many hours has it been since midnight?

questions.hint: First read the time on the clock. Then count the hours from midnight to midday, and from midday to that time.

steps.explain: Read the time. The short (hour) hand points to 5 and the long (minute) hand points to 12.
steps.work: The time is 5 o’clock.

steps.explain: It is afternoon, so it is 5 pm. Count the hours since midnight in two parts.
steps.work:
Midnight to midday: \(12\) hours

Midday to 5 pm: \(5\) hours

steps.explain: Add the two parts.
Check: 5 hours would be the time since midday, and 15 or 16 hours would be 3 pm or 4 pm.
steps.work: The answer is B.

keyPoints.note: In the afternoon, add 12 hours to the clock time to count the hours since midnight.
Midnight is 12:00 at night. Count from there.

steps.explain: Write the calculation. The brackets are needed so that all the notes are added before dividing.
Check the other options.
steps.work:
A: \((185)\times5=925\) — multiplying makes the amount bigger, it does not share it.

B: with no brackets only the last note \(5\) is divided by \(5\) (division is done first): \(100+50+20+10+1=181\).

D: \((100+50+20+10+5)\times5\) multiplies instead of dividing.

steps.explain: Only option C shows the total shared equally between five children.
steps.work: The answer is C.

Divide by 5, after finding the total of all the notes.

questions.stem:
Questions 11 and 12 refer to the following information.

The chart below shows where 100 coffee drinkers had their first cup of coffee on a typical day. The numbers in the table are decimals.

| Where | Share of coffee drinkers |
|---|---|
| At home | 0.7 |
| At work | 0.17 |
| While travelling | 0.08 |
| Coffee shop | 0.04 |
| Other | 0.01 |

parts.stem: Which statement is correct about where people had their first cup of coffee?
options: Most people had their first cup of coffee at their home or at work.
Most people had their first cup of coffee at their work or at a coffee shop.
Most people had their first cup of coffee at their home or while travelling.
Most people had their first cup of coffee at their home or at a coffee shop.
parts.hint: A decimal like 0.7 means 7 tenths, or 70 out of 100. Find the two biggest numbers in the table. Which two places do they belong to?

steps.explain: Change each decimal into “out of 100” so that it is easy to compare.

steps.explain: Add them to see how many people that is.
steps.work: \(70+17=87\) out of 100 — most of the coffee drinkers.

steps.explain: Check the other options.
steps.work:
B: work + coffee shop \(=17+4=21\)

C: home + travelling \(=70+8=78\) (home is right, but travelling is not the 2nd biggest)

D: home + coffee shop \(=70+4=74\)

Only “home or at work” (87) is the two biggest groups. The answer is A.

parts.stem: Assume that the figures in the table are correct for all groups of coffee drinkers. Out of 50 coffee drinkers, about how many would say they had their first cup of coffee at a coffee shop?
parts.hint: The table says 0.04 of 100 drinkers use a coffee shop. 50 is half of 100, so how many of the 4 would there be?

steps.explain: Find the coffee shop share in the table.

questions.stem: Every day from Monday to Friday, Anthony works from 7.30 am until 4.30 pm (including breaks for morning and afternoon tea plus lunch). How many hours is he at work altogether, including breaks?
questions.hint: First find how many hours Anthony is at work in ONE day. Then work out how many days he works.

steps.explain: Find the length of one working day: from 7.30 am to 4.30 pm.
steps.work:
7.30 am to 12.30 pm is \(5\) hours.

12.30 pm to 4.30 pm is \(4\) hours.

\(5+4=9\) hours each day

steps.explain: Count the days: Monday to Friday is 5 days.
steps.work: \(9\) hours \(\times\) \(5\) days

questions.stem: Which calculation shows you how to find the number of hundreds in 39 000?
questions.hint: To find how many hundreds fit into a number, ask: how many groups of 100 can you make from it? Which operation finds the number of groups?

steps.explain: “How many hundreds in 39 000?” means how many groups of 100 make up 39 000. Finding the number of groups is division.
Work it out and check with multiplication.
Check the other options.
steps.work:
A: \(39\,000\times100=3\,900\,000\) — far too big.

C: one-tenth of \(39\,000\) is \(3\,900\), and \(3\,900\times100=390\,000\) — too big.

D: \(100\div39\,000\) is a tiny number, much less than 1.

steps.explain: There are 390 hundreds in 39 000, found by dividing by 100.
steps.work: The answer is B.

keyPoints.note: This is a “how many groups” question. Groups are found by dividing.

questions.hint: Look at two things in each picture: how many shapes there are, and which way the shapes are turned.

steps.explain: Count the shapes in each picture.
steps.work: I has 1 shape, II has 2, III has 3 and IV has 4. The next picture must have 5 shapes.

questions.stem: In which general direction would you travel if you went directly from Sydney to Singapore?
questions.hint: Picture a map with north at the top. Is Singapore above or below Sydney, and is it to the left or to the right?

steps.explain: Picture a map of the world. Sydney is in the south of the world (southern hemisphere). Singapore is close to the equator.
steps.work: Singapore is NORTH of Sydney. (It is closer to the equator, so it is higher up the map.)

steps.explain: Is Singapore to the left (west) or to the right (east) of Sydney?
steps.work: Singapore is on the left of Sydney on a map: WEST of Sydney (Singapore is about 104° east, Sydney is about 151° east).

steps.explain: Put the two directions together.
steps.work: north + west = north-west

steps.explain: Check the other options.
steps.work: north-east and north-west differ by whether Singapore is left or right. “North” alone and “west” alone each ignore one of the two directions.

steps.explain: The answer is A.

keyPoints.note: A general direction can be a mix, like north-west, if the place is both north and west.

questions.stem: There are 53 pupils who have to be divided into groups. The teacher first tries to divide them into 8 equal groups but there are some pupils left over. How many pupils would be left after the 8 groups?
questions.hint: Divide 53 by 8. How many pupils go into each group, and how many are left over? Use your 8 times table.

steps.explain: Find the biggest number that 8 groups can be made of, without going over 53 pupils. Use the 8 times table.
steps.work: \(8\times6=48\)   \(8\times7=56\) — too many.

steps.explain: So each group has 6 pupils, and 48 pupils are in groups.
The pupils left over are the ones not in a group.
Check: 48 + 5 = 53 ✓. The answer is B.

keyPoints.note: Make as many equal groups as you can, and count the ones that do not fit.
The pupils left over are the remainder.

questions.stem:
Which number comes next in the series?

21  42  84  ?
questions.hint: Look at how the numbers change. Is something being added each time (the gaps are 21, 42, …), or are the numbers being multiplied?

steps.explain: The gaps are not the same (21, then 42), so look at multiplying.

questions.stem: Angela paid \(\$378\) in advance for her school fees and \(\$24\) for books. The school reduced the school fees to \(\$262.00\). How much will the school now refund to Angela?
questions.hint: A refund is money given back. Compare what Angela paid for school fees with what the school fees now cost. Does the cost of books matter?

steps.explain: Find the facts about the school fees only. The books were paid for separately and their price did not change.
steps.work:
Paid for fees: \(\$378\)

Fees now: \(\$262\)

(The \(\$24\) for books is not part of the refund.)

steps.explain: The refund is the difference between what she paid and what the fees now are.
Check by adding back.
Check the other options: \(\$670\) adds the books and the new fees together, \(\$216\) and \(\$140\) come from subtracting the wrong amounts.
steps.work: The answer is A.

keyPoints.note: The refund is the difference between the old and new fee.
A refund is money given back. Which amounts does the school give back?

questions.stem: In the city, Anthony travelled 107 km on half a tank of petrol. How far could he travel on a full tank? Show the correct calculation.
questions.hint: A full tank is how many times more than half a tank? Which operation gives that many times as far?

steps.explain: Compare a full tank with half a tank.
steps.work: A full tank is TWICE half a tank (two halves make a whole).

steps.explain: He travels 107 km on each half tank, so double it.
Check each option by working it out.
Only option B is a correct calculation.
steps.work: The answer is B.

keyPoints.note: A full tank is two half tanks.
Work out each option: only the correct one really equals 214.

questions.stem: The date today is the 6th February 1999. Angelena was born on the 5th April 1955. How old would she be today?
questions.hint: Count whole years from her birth date to her last birthday. Then count the months from that birthday to today. Has her birthday in 1999 happened yet?

steps.explain: Find her age in whole years. Her birthday is on 5 April. In 1999 it is only February, so her 1999 birthday has not happened yet.
steps.work:
Her last birthday was 5 April 1998.

1998 − 1955 = 43 years

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 360 122" width="95%" height="auto" font-family="system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Arial,sans-serif"><line x1="20" y1="70" x2="340" y2="70" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="2.4" /><line x1="24" y1="62" x2="24" y2="78" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="3" /><line x1="210" y1="62" x2="210" y2="78" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="3" /><line x1="300" y1="62" x2="300" y2="78" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="3" /><text x="24" y="96" font-size="10.5" font-weight="700" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="start" >5 Apr 1955</text><text x="24" y="110" font-size="10" font-weight="600" fill="#64748b" text-anchor="start" >born</text><text x="212" y="96" font-size="10.5" font-weight="700" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >5 Apr 1998</text><text x="212" y="110" font-size="10" font-weight="600" fill="#64748b" text-anchor="middle" >43rd birthday... 43 years</text><text x="332" y="96" font-size="10.5" font-weight="700" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="end" >6 Feb 1999</text><text x="332" y="110" font-size="10" font-weight="600" fill="#64748b" text-anchor="end" >today</text><path d="M24 60 Q117 10 212 60" fill="none" stroke="#4338ca" stroke-width="2.4"/><text x="118" y="30" font-size="12.5" font-weight="800" fill="#4338ca" text-anchor="middle" >43 years</text></svg>

steps.explain: Count the months from her last birthday (5 April 1998) to today (6 February 1999).
steps.work:
5 Apr → 5 May (1) → 5 Jun (2) → 5 Jul (3) → 5 Aug (4) → 5 Sep (5) → 5 Oct (6) → 5 Nov (7) → 5 Dec (8) → 5 Jan (9) → 5 Feb (10)

That is 10 months, and 6 February is 1 day after 5 February.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 360 122" width="95%" height="auto" font-family="system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Arial,sans-serif"><line x1="20" y1="70" x2="340" y2="70" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="2.4" /><line x1="24" y1="62" x2="24" y2="78" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="3" /><line x1="210" y1="62" x2="210" y2="78" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="3" /><line x1="300" y1="62" x2="300" y2="78" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="3" /><text x="24" y="96" font-size="10.5" font-weight="700" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="start" >5 Apr 1955</text><text x="24" y="110" font-size="10" font-weight="600" fill="#64748b" text-anchor="start" >born</text><text x="212" y="96" font-size="10.5" font-weight="700" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >5 Apr 1998</text><text x="212" y="110" font-size="10" font-weight="600" fill="#64748b" text-anchor="middle" >43rd birthday... 43 years</text><text x="332" y="96" font-size="10.5" font-weight="700" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="end" >6 Feb 1999</text><text x="332" y="110" font-size="10" font-weight="600" fill="#64748b" text-anchor="end" >today</text><path d="M24 60 Q117 10 212 60" fill="none" stroke="#4338ca" stroke-width="2.4"/><text x="118" y="30" font-size="12.5" font-weight="800" fill="#4338ca" text-anchor="middle" >43 years</text><path d="M212 60 Q276 34 336 60" fill="none" stroke="#059669" stroke-width="2.4"/><text x="276" y="28" font-size="12" font-weight="800" fill="#059669" text-anchor="middle" >10 months + 1 day</text></svg>

steps.explain: Put the years and months together.
steps.work: 43 years + 10 months (and 1 day) \(\approx\) 43 years 10 months

steps.explain: Check the other options: 44 years would need her birthday to have passed (it is not yet April), and 9 months would stop at 5 January.
steps.work: The answer is D.

keyPoints.text: How old would she be today
keyPoints.note: Check whether her birthday this year has happened yet before you count the years.

questions.stem: I had a meal with Terry and his wife at a Mexican restaurant. The cost came to \(\$51.00\) and I added a tip of ten per cent (10%), making it \(\$56.10\). Which is the correct calculation for the answer of \(\$56.10\)?
questions.hint: The tip is worked out on the cost of the meal. Find 10% of the meal, then add it to the meal cost.

steps.explain: Find 10% of the cost of the meal. 10% is the same as one-tenth, so divide by 10.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 360 72" width="85%" height="auto" font-family="system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Arial,sans-serif"><path d="M10 24 L10 18 L350 18 L350 24" fill="none" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="1.4"/><text x="180.0" y="13" font-size="13" font-weight="700" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >$56.10 altogether</text><rect x="10" y="30" width="309.09090909090907" height="34" rx="4" fill="#dbeafe" stroke="#4f46e5" stroke-width="1.6" /><text x="164.54545454545453" y="52.0" font-size="13" font-weight="700" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >meal $51.00</text><rect x="319.09090909090907" y="30" width="30.909090909090903" height="34" rx="4" fill="#fef3c7" stroke="#4f46e5" stroke-width="1.6" /><text x="334.5454545454545" y="52.0" font-size="13" font-weight="700" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >tip $5.10</text></svg>

steps.explain: Add the tip to the cost of the meal.
So the calculation is the meal cost plus 10% of the meal cost.
Check the other options.
steps.work:
A: \(10\%\) of \(56.10\) is the tip on the total, which is not how the tip was found.

C and D use \(51.45\), which is not an amount in the question.

steps.explain: The answer is B.

keyPoints.note: A 10% tip is worked out from the cost of the meal, then added to it.

questions.stem: What is the area of this space?

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 484 458" width="55%" height="auto"><image href="/oc/t3-q26.jpg" x="0" y="0" width="484" height="458"/></svg>

questions.hint: Imagine the full 6 cm by 6 cm square first. Then take away the piece that is missing in the bottom-left corner.

steps.explain: Look at the shape. It is a 6 cm by 6 cm square with a corner piece missing. The top is 6 cm wide, the bottom is 5 cm wide, and the left side is 3 cm + 3 cm = 6 cm.
steps.work: full square: \(6\times6=36\) sq cm

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 242 214" width="55%" height="auto" font-family="system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Arial,sans-serif"><rect x="36" y="30" width="156" height="156" rx="0" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><polygon points="36,30 192,30 192,186 62,186 62,108 36,108" fill="#e0e7ff" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="2.2" stroke-linejoin="round" /><text x="127.0" y="108" font-size="15" font-weight="800" fill="#4338ca" text-anchor="middle" >6 × 6 = 36</text></svg>

steps.explain: Find the size of the missing piece. The bottom is 1 cm shorter than the top (6 − 5 = 1 cm) and the missing part is 3 cm tall.
steps.work: missing piece: \(1\times3=3\) sq cm

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 242 214" width="55%" height="auto" font-family="system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Arial,sans-serif"><rect x="36" y="30" width="156" height="156" rx="0" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><polygon points="36,30 192,30 192,186 62,186 62,108 36,108" fill="#e0e7ff" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="2.2" stroke-linejoin="round" /><rect x="36" y="108" width="26" height="78" rx="0" fill="#fef3c7" stroke="#f59e0b" stroke-width="2.2" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><text x="49.0" y="149.6" font-size="11" font-weight="800" fill="#b45309" text-anchor="middle" >1×3</text><text x="127.0" y="108" font-size="15" font-weight="800" fill="#4338ca" text-anchor="middle" >33 sq cm</text></svg>

Check another way: split into a 6 by 3 rectangle and a 5 by 3 rectangle.
The answer is A.

keyPoints.note: Area is the amount of surface inside the shape, measured in square centimetres.

questions.hint: Find the perimeter of each shape by adding up all of its sides. For the shape in Question 26, add every side, including the little step.

steps.explain: Perimeter of the new shape: it is a square with sides of 6 cm. It has 4 equal sides.

steps.explain: Perimeter of the shape in Question 26: add all six sides going around the outside.
steps.work:
\(6+6+5+3+1+3=24\) cm

top 6, right side 3 + 3 = 6, bottom 5, up the notch 3, across the step 1, up the left side 3.

steps.explain: Compare the two perimeters.
steps.work: \(24-24=0\) cm. The notch takes 1 cm off the bottom, but adds 1 cm of step and the 3 cm sides stay the same length, so the perimeter does not change.

steps.explain: The difference is 0 cm.
steps.work: The answer is B.

Subtract one perimeter from the other.

questions.stem: How far (in sea miles) would a steamship like the Mauretania travelling at a speed of 27 knots cover in three hours?
questions.hint: A speed of 27 knots means 27 sea miles every hour. Work out the distance for 3 hours.

steps.explain: A knot is one sea mile per hour, so 27 knots means the ship travels 27 sea miles in each hour.
steps.work: After each hour the ship has gone another \(27\) sea miles.

steps.explain: Multiply the distance in one hour by the number of hours.
steps.work: distance \(=\) speed \(\times\) time \(=27\times3\)

steps.explain: Calculate.
steps.work: \(27\times3=20\times3+7\times3=60+21=81\) sea miles

steps.explain: Check the other options: 54 is two hours, and 71 and 91 are not multiples of 27.
steps.work: The answer is A.

keyPoints.note: A speed in knots is the number of sea miles travelled in one hour.
Multiply the distance travelled in one hour by 3.

questions.stem: Homer was a famous epic poet. He lived around 700 BC. How would you calculate the number of years from 700 BC to the year 2000?
questions.hint: BC years count backwards towards the year 0. Draw a time line with 700 BC on the left, year 0 in the middle and 2000 on the right.

steps.explain: Draw a time line. 700 BC is before the year 0, so it is 700 years to the left of 0. The year 2000 is 2000 years to the right of 0.
steps.work: The year 0 splits the time line into two parts.

steps.explain: Find the length of each part.
steps.work:
700 BC to year 0: \(700\) years

year 0 to 2000: \(2000\) years

steps.explain: Add the two parts together.

steps.explain: Check the other options.
steps.work:
A: \(2000+(2000-700)=3300\) — adds the wrong amounts.

B: \(700+(2000-700)=2000\) — does not count from 700 BC.

D: \(2000-700=1300\) would be the answer if both years were AD (after the year 0), but 700 BC is before the year 0.

steps.explain: The answer is C.

keyPoints.note: BC means before the year 0, so the years are on the other side of 0 from 2000.
Add the years before year 0 to the years after year 0.

questions.stem:
Questions 11 and 12 refer to the following information.

These are the chances of winning that have been quoted for different types of gambling. These figures show the chances of winning the first prize.

| Gambling | Chances |
|---|---|
| Jackpot \(\$2\) | 1 in 180 000 |
| Jackpot \(\$5\) | 1 in 140 000 |
| Lotto Strike | 1 in 3.2 million |
| Lucky 7 | 1 in 200 000 |
| Oz Lotto | 1 in 8 million |
| Pools | 1 in 3.8 million |
| Powerball | 1 in 25 million |
| Scratchie \(\$2\) | 1 in 480 000 |

parts.hint: “1 in 25 million” means you have to be very lucky: only one ticket in 25 million wins. The bigger the number after “1 in”, the worse the chance. Which number is biggest?

steps.explain: Each chance is written as “1 in …”. The more tickets there are for each winner, the harder it is to win.
steps.work: “1 in 140 000” is much easier than “1 in 25 million”.

steps.explain: Change the “million” numbers to ordinary numbers so that they are easy to compare.

steps.work: The biggest number is 1 in 25 million: Powerball.

questions.stem:
Which number comes next in this series?

128  64  32  ?
questions.hint: The numbers are getting smaller. Is the same amount taken away each time, or is something else happening?

steps.explain: Compare neighbouring numbers.
steps.work: \(128\to64\) is half. \(64\to32\) is half. (The amounts taken away, 64 and 32, are not the same.)

questions.stem:
Look at the desks which are numbered from A to Y in the chart below.

The pupil in seat V moves three desks forward and changes places.
The pupil in seat W moves three desks to the left then one desk forward and changes places.
The pupil in seat X moves three desks forward and changes places.
The pupil in seat Y moves two seats forward and three across and changes places.

Which pupil is now in seat I?

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 605 308" width="80%" height="auto"><image href="/oc/t4-q17.jpg" x="0" y="0" width="605" height="308"/></svg>

questions.hint: “Forward” means towards the top row of the chart. Follow each move to see which seat each pupil goes to. Which move ends at seat I?

steps.explain: “Forward” means up the chart, towards row A–F. Find where each pupil moves to.
steps.work: V is in the bottom row, third from the left.

questions.stem: One of the longest tennis games ever played at Wimbledon was in 1969. It took around 5¼ hours. R. Gonzales (USA) beat C. Pasarell (USA), losing 22 to 24 in the first set; then losing 1 to 6 in the second set; winning 16 to 14 in the third set; winning 6 to 3 in the fourth set; and winning 11 to 9 in the fifth set. How do you calculate the number of games played by Gonzales?
questions.hint: In each set, Gonzales’s score is written first (“losing 22 to 24” means he scored 22 games and Pasarell 24). Add up Gonzales’s number in each of the five sets.

steps.explain: Write down the score of each set. Gonzales’s score is the first number each time.
steps.work:
Set 1: 22 to 24 (Gonzales 22)

Set 2: 1 to 6 (Gonzales 1)

Set 3: 16 to 14 (Gonzales 16)

Set 4: 6 to 3 (Gonzales 6)

Set 5: 11 to 9 (Gonzales 11)

steps.explain: Add up Gonzales’s games from all five sets.
Check each option by working it out.
steps.work:
A: \(56+56=112\) is the games of BOTH players together.

C: \(22+1+16+6+11=56\), not \(58\).

D: \(24+6+14+3+9=56\) adds Pasarell’s games, not Gonzales’s.

steps.explain: Only option B adds up Gonzales’s own games.
steps.work: The answer is B.

keyPoints.text: number of games played by Gonzales
keyPoints.note: Use only Gonzales’s number in each set, then add them all.

questions.stem: These are the sides of a box. They are folded so that the side with the star is at the top. Which side will now be at the bottom of the box?

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 583 600" width="70%" height="auto"><image href="/oc/t4-q27.jpg" x="0" y="0" width="583" height="600"/></svg>

questions.hint: In a flat net, a row of four squares wraps around the box. In that row, the square two places away from the star is on the opposite side of the box.

steps.work: Faces that are opposite each other in the box are the ones that end up on opposite sides.

questions.stem: USA coins usually come in 1 cents, 5 cents, 10 cents, and 25 cents. I have to pay the salesperson \(\$1.07\). What is the least number of coins that I can give him/her?
questions.hint: To use the fewest coins, start with the biggest coin (25 cents) as many times as you can. Then use the next biggest coin for what is left.

steps.explain: Change the money to cents so that it is easy to work with.
Use as many 25-cent coins as you can without going over 107 cents.
steps.work:
\(4\times25=100\), and \(5\times25=125\) is too much.

So use four 25c coins. \(107-100=7\) cents are still to pay.

steps.explain: Pay the last 7 cents with the fewest coins. A 10c coin is too big, so use one 5c coin and then 1c coins.
steps.work: \(7=5+1+1\): one 5c coin and two 1c coins.

questions.stem: John works at the M & C Deli. He earns \(\$5.48\) an hour. He works three hours on Monday and three hours on Wednesday. How much does he earn each week?
questions.hint: First find the total number of hours John works in a week. Then multiply by the amount he earns in one hour. Check that the answer to each calculation is really right.

steps.explain: Find the total hours he works in a week.
steps.work: 3 hours on Monday + 3 hours on Wednesday \(=3\times2=6\) hours

steps.explain: He earns \(\$5.48\) for each hour, so multiply by the hours.
Write the calculation in the same form as the options.
Check the other options by working them out.
steps.work:
A: \(5.48\times3\times2=32.88\), not \(34.88\) — the calculation is right but the answer is wrong.

B: \(16.44\times3=49.32\), not \(32.88\).

D: \(5.48\times6=32.88\), not \(34.88\).

steps.explain: Only option C has a correct calculation and a correct answer.
steps.work: The answer is C.

keyPoints.text: three hours on Monday and three hours on Wednesday
keyPoints.note: Add up the hours first: that is 3 × 2.
Multiply the total hours by the pay for one hour.

questions.stem:
At the university, the rate for mileage allowance is around 53 cents per kilometre. This is the kilometre reading at the beginning of a trip.

6 3 5 0 4

And this is the reading at the end of a trip.

6 3 5 3 4

How much mileage allowance should be paid?
questions.hint: First find how many kilometres were travelled: subtract the start reading from the end reading. Then multiply by 53 cents.

steps.explain: Find the distance travelled: end reading take away start reading.
steps.work: \(63\,534-63\,504=30\) km. Only the tens digit changed (0 to 3), so the trip was 30 km.

questions.stem:
Which is the correct way to solve this problem?

\(3\times8+6\div2=\;?\)
options: multiply 3 by 8 then add this answer to 6 and divide it all by 2
divide 6 by 2 then multiply 3 by 8; then add the two answers
multiply 3 by 14 (8 + 6) then divide the answer by 2
divide 14 (8 + 6) by 2 then multiply that answer by 3
questions.hint: Remember the rule for the order of operations: do multiplication and division first, then addition and subtraction. Which parts of the sum are multiplication or division?

steps.explain: Find the operations in the sum.
steps.work: \(3\times8\) is a multiplication, \(6\div2\) is a division, and the \(+\) in the middle is an addition.

steps.explain: Multiplication and division are done first (in either order). Addition is done last.
Now do the addition with the two answers.
Check the other options.
steps.work:
A: \(24+6=30\), then \(30\div2=15\) — it adds before dividing.

C: \(3\times14=42\), \(42\div2=21\) — adds \(8+6\) first.

D: \(14\div2=7\), \(7\times3=21\) — adds \(8+6\) first.

steps.explain: Only option B follows the order of operations (and gives 27).
steps.work: The answer is B.

keyPoints.text: correct way to solve this problem
keyPoints.note: Multiplication and division come before addition.

questions.stem: An area of 243 hectares has to be divided into nine equal lots. How many hectares would there be for each of the lots?
questions.hint: Dividing into equal lots means dividing by 9. How many times does 9 fit into 243? Try your 9 times table.

steps.explain: Dividing 243 hectares into 9 equal lots means dividing by 9.
Work it out in steps. How many 9s are in 24? Then in the rest?
steps.work:
\(9\times2=18\), and \(24-18=6\), then bring down the 3 to make \(63\).

\(9\times7=63\), so \(243\div9=27\).

steps.explain: Check by multiplying back.
Check the other options: 26 × 9 = 234, 30 × 9 = 270 and 33 × 9 = 297. Only 27 gives 243.
steps.work: The answer is B.

keyPoints.note: Dividing into equal lots means dividing by the number of lots.

questions.stem: Jim owed David Jones \(\$288.85\) last month. He paid David Jones \(\$113.95\) and spent another \(\$79.95\) this month. How do you calculate how much he owes David Jones now?
questions.hint: Think about whether each amount makes the debt bigger or smaller. Paying money back reduces what he owes. Spending more at the shop increases it.

steps.explain: Start with what Jim owed at the beginning.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 360 72" width="85%" height="auto" font-family="system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Arial,sans-serif"><path d="M10 24 L10 18 L350 18 L350 24" fill="none" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="1.4"/><text x="180.0" y="13" font-size="13" font-weight="700" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >at the start</text><rect x="10" y="30" width="340.0" height="34" rx="4" fill="#fee2e2" stroke="#4f46e5" stroke-width="1.6" /><text x="180.0" y="52.0" font-size="13" font-weight="700" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >owed $288.85</text></svg>

steps.explain: He PAID David Jones \(\$113.95\). Paying back means he owes LESS, so take it away.
He SPENT another \(\$79.95\) at the shop. Spending more means he owes MORE, so add it.

steps.work:
He now owes \(\$254.85\).

A takes both amounts away (\(\$95.05\)), B adds both (\(\$482.75\)), and D starts with the small amounts, so each is wrong.

steps.explain: The answer is C.

keyPoints.note: Paying money back makes the amount owed smaller: subtract.
Spending more makes the amount owed bigger: add.

This chart shows the typical costs for a textbook of around 250 pages. The book sells for \(\$40.00\). Half of the \(\$40.00\) goes to the bookseller.

BOOK PROFITS FOR A TYPICAL 250 PAGE BOOK

| Cost | Amount |
|---|---|
| Printing and bookbinding | \(\$3.20\) |
| Warehouse and distribution | \(\$3.20\) |
| Bookseller | \(\$20.00\) |
| Rent, salaries | \(\$3.20\) |
| Advertisements | \(\$2.40\) |
| Author’s payment | \(\$4.00\) |
| Publisher’s profit | \(\$4.00\) |
| TOTAL | \(\$40.00\) |

Source: Adapted from Anne R. Carey & Jerry Mosemak, USA Today, October 1998

Printing and bookbinding, warehouse and distribution, rent and salaries, and advertisements are the publisher’s costs.

questions.stem: This week John worked on Tuesday, Wednesday and Friday from 4 pm until 7 pm at a delicatessen. How many hours did he work this week?
questions.hint: First find how long John works each day. Then find how many days he works.

steps.explain: Find the hours in one working day: from 4 pm to 7 pm.
Find how many days he works: Tuesday, Wednesday and Friday.
Multiply the hours each day by the days.
steps.work: \(3\text{ hours}\times3\text{ days}=9\text{ hours}\)

questions.stem: Each day I drink a 375 ml can of soft drink in the summer. Which calculation shows how many LITRES I drink over 12 weeks?
questions.hint: Work in steps: how many days are in 12 weeks, then how many millilitres in total, then change millilitres into litres.

steps.explain: Find the number of days in 12 weeks.
steps.work: 1 week \(=7\) days, so 12 weeks \(=12\times7=84\) days.

steps.explain: Find the total number of millilitres. One can a day for 84 days.
steps.work: \(375\text{ ml}\times84\) days

steps.explain: Change millilitres into litres. There are 1000 ml in 1 litre, so divide by 1000.
Check the other options.
steps.work: A multiplies by \(1000\) and divides by \(84\) (the wrong way round). C uses 12 (weeks) instead of 84 (days). D does not use the 375 ml correctly.

steps.explain: The answer is B.

keyPoints.text: how many LITRES I drink over 12 weeks
keyPoints.note: Weeks must be changed into days, and millilitres into litres.

questions.stem: How many square tiles, that are 10 cm long, can you fit into a space that is 200 cm by 200 cm?
questions.hint: First find how many tiles fit along one side of the space. Then think about how many rows of tiles you need.

steps.explain: Find how many 10 cm tiles fit along one side.

questions.stem: An object falls to the ground at around 9 metres per second. How long would it take to fall from a plane that was 9 000 metres in the air?
questions.hint: First find how many seconds it takes. Then change seconds into minutes by dividing by 60.

steps.explain: The object falls 9 metres every second. Find how many seconds it takes to fall 9 000 metres.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 300 144" width="80%" height="auto" font-family="system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Arial,sans-serif"><line x1="30" y1="20" x2="30" y2="120" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="2" /><text x="30" y="14" font-size="11" font-weight="700" fill="#64748b" text-anchor="middle" >plane</text><text x="30" y="136" font-size="11" font-weight="700" fill="#64748b" text-anchor="middle" >ground</text><line x1="26" y1="40" x2="34" y2="40" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.4" /><line x1="26" y1="60" x2="34" y2="60" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.4" /><line x1="26" y1="80" x2="34" y2="80" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.4" /><line x1="26" y1="100" x2="34" y2="100" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.4" /><line x1="26" y1="120" x2="34" y2="120" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.4" /><text x="150" y="40" font-size="13" font-weight="800" fill="#4338ca" text-anchor="middle" >9 000 m to fall</text><text x="150" y="62" font-size="12.5" font-weight="700" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >9 m every second</text><text x="150" y="86" font-size="13" font-weight="800" fill="#059669" text-anchor="middle" >9 000 ÷ 9 = 1 000 seconds</text><text x="150" y="108" font-size="12" font-weight="700" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >1 000 ÷ 60 = 16 r 40 → between</text><text x="150" y="124" font-size="13" font-weight="800" fill="#059669" text-anchor="middle" >16 and 17 minutes</text></svg>

steps.explain: Change seconds into minutes. There are 60 seconds in one minute.
16 full minutes use up 960 seconds, and there are 40 more seconds.
steps.work:
\(16\times60=960\)   \(1\,000-960=40\)

So the time is 16 minutes and 40 seconds, which is between 16 and 17 minutes.

steps.explain: Check the other options: 26–27 minutes would be 1 560–1 620 seconds, and 9–10 and 6–7 minutes are far too short.
steps.work: The answer is B.

keyPoints.note: This tells you how far it falls in one second.
The answer is in minutes, but you will first get seconds.

questions.stem:
Which number comes next in this series?

questions.hint: The numbers are getting smaller quickly. Check whether each number is a third of the one before.
